posts.title: On Faith, Wellness, and Reality…
posts.description: Photo credit: https://www.sjcfl.us/employee-connection/wellness/ One of the questions the bishop asks a priest in their ordination vows is, “Will you do your best to pattern your life and that of your family in accordance with the teachings of Christ, so that you may be a wholesome example to your people?” I remember when my bishop asked me that question over 16 years ago how daunting that question felt – not only for myself but also for my family. Having grown up as a preacher’s kid, I remember thinking how much pressure that invitation felt: for the whole family to be a wholesome example to the church. So, when the Church invited clergy and their spouses to attend a Wellness Conference last week, focusing on both physical and financial wellness, I had a revelation in one of those sessions: this is what that promise was all about. posts.title: Sermon – Matthew 22.15-22, P24, YA, October 18, 2026
posts.description: “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Jesus says these words today, and we tend immediately do some mental math to make meaning. As one scholar points out, “Some people point to this passage as proof that God and politics should be kept separate — that things like taxes have absolutely nothing to do with one’s theological commitments. Others say that this story proves that religion is a matter of the heart, and that Jesus doesn’t really care about mundane things like what you do with your money. And some have cited this passage as proof that Jesus taught that the law is the law, and our duty as Christians is to support the government no matter what.” [i] But before we start doing our own twenty-first century mental math, we need to understand what is happening in today’s story that evokes this seemingly clear statement, “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’

posts.title: On Hidden Blessings…
posts.description: Photo credit: Jennifer Andrews-Weckerly; reuse with permission only. This week I got a last minute invitation: a friend of our parish is building a new home for their family, and the house is finally framed and closed in. In a matter of days, the drywall will be hung. In that brief window, the friend sent out an SOS to friends of faith – come by and write a scripture verse, a blessing, a prayer, or a book quote on the studs before they are hidden away by drywall, tape, paint, and artwork. In looking around the house, and all those words of blessing and care, I was thinking about how much a house hides. All those words of blessing will be hidden very soon. But eventually, those walls will also witness life’s sorrows and joys, life’s heartbreaks and cheers, life’s hardships and abundance. Someday, new generations will warm the home with their squeals and laughter. Renovations may be made, new paint may be applied, new pictures may be hung.
